content: 1. Dilution Techniques: Quantitative methods are employed to determine the minimal inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of antimicrobial agents. These MICs provide consistent and reproducible measurements of bacterial susceptibility to antimicrobial compounds. The determination of MICs should be conducted using standardized test methods, such as broth or agar dilution techniques. The interpretation of MIC values must adhere to established criteria. 2. Diffusion Techniques: Quantitative methods that involve measuring the diameters of inhibition zones also yield reproducible estimates of bacterial susceptibility to antimicrobial agents. The size of the inhibition zone serves as an indicator of bacterial susceptibility. This measurement should be performed using a standardized test method. In this procedure, paper disks impregnated with 30 mcg of cefuroxime axetil are used to assess the susceptibility of microorganisms to cefuroxime axetil. The interpretive criteria for disk diffusion testing are provided in the relevant guidelines. 3. The susceptibility of Staphylococci to cefuroxime axetil can be inferred from testing only penicillin and either cefoxitin or oxacillin. 4. The susceptibility of Streptococcus pyogenes can be deduced from penicillin testing alone. 5. A report of Susceptible indicates that the antimicrobial agent is likely to inhibit the growth of the pathogen if it achieves the necessary concentration at the site of infection. A report of Intermediate suggests that the result is equivocal, and further testing may be required if alternative, clinically viable drugs are not fully effective. This category may have clinical relevance in body sites where the drug is physiologically concentrated or when high dosages can be administered. It also provides a buffer zone to account for minor technical variations. A report of Resistant indicates that the antimicrobial agent is unlikely to inhibit pathogen growth at achievable concentrations at the infection site, and alternative therapy should be considered. 6. Standardized susceptibility testing procedures require the use of laboratory controls to ensure the accuracy and precision of reagents, supplies, and the techniques of the individual performing the test. Quality control (QC) ranges for MIC and disk diffusion testing using the 30 mcg disk are provided in the guidelines. Pharmacokinetics 1. Absorption and Metabolism: After oral administration, cefuroxime axetil is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract and rapidly hydrolyzed by nonspecific esterases in the intestinal mucosa and blood to its active form, cefuroxime. Cefuroxime is then distributed throughout extracellular fluids. The axetil moiety is metabolized into acetaldehyde and acetic acid. 2. Approximately 50% of serum cefuroxime is bound to plasma proteins. Pharmacokinetic parameters for cefuroxime axetil tablets and oral suspension are detailed in the respective tables. 3. A 250 mg/5 mL dose of cefuroxime axetil suspension is bioequivalent to two 125 mg/5 mL doses of the suspension when administered with food. However, cefuroxime axetil suspension is not bioequivalent to cefuroxime axetil tablets in healthy adults. The tablet and suspension formulations are not interchangeable on a milligram-per-milligram basis. The area under the curve (AUC) for the suspension averages 91% of that for the tablet, and the peak plasma concentration for the suspension averages 71% of that for the tablet. Consequently, the safety and efficacy of both formulations were established in separate clinical trials. 4. The absorption of cefuroxime axetil tablets is enhanced when taken with food, increasing the absolute bioavailability from 37% to 52%. Despite this difference, clinical and bacteriological responses were not affected by food intake during tablet administration in studies where this was evaluated. 5. All pharmacokinetic, clinical effectiveness, and safety studies in pediatric patients using the suspension formulation were conducted in the fed state. No data are available on the absorption kinetics of the suspension in fasted pediatric patients. 6. Cefuroxime is excreted unchanged in the urine. In adults, approximately 50% of the administered dose is recovered in the urine within 12 hours. The pharmacokinetics of cefuroxime in the urine of pediatric patients have not been studied. Until further data are available, renal pharmacokinetic properties established in adults should not be extrapolated to pediatric patients. 7. In a study of 28 adults with normal and severely impaired renal function, the elimination half-life of cefuroxime was prolonged in proportion to the severity of renal impairment. In a study of 16 adult hemodialysis patients with end-stage renal disease, the majority of a cefuroxime dose was removed by hemodialysis within 5 hours. Despite reduced elimination in geriatric patients, dosage adjustment based on age is not necessary. Nonclinical Toxicology There is limited information available regarding the nonclinical toxicology of cefuroxime axetil in the drug label. Clinical Studies 1. Cefuroxime Axetil Tablets: A well-controlled clinical study was conducted in patients with acute bacterial maxillary sinusitis. Each patient underwent maxillary sinus aspiration via sinus puncture before initiating treatment for presumed acute bacterial sinusitis. Radiographic and clinical evidence of acute maxillary sinusitis was required for inclusion. The study demonstrated that the clinical effectiveness of cefuroxime axetil tablets was comparable to an oral antimicrobial agent containing a beta-lactamase inhibitor in treating acute maxillary sinusitis. However, sufficient microbiological data were obtained to confirm the effectiveness of cefuroxime axetil tablets specifically in treating acute bacterial maxillary sinusitis caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae or non-beta-lactamase-producing Haemophilus influenzae.
